> [!abstract] Key idea
> A **wideband FSS** blocks a wide range of frequencies. This design puts **a different pattern on each face** of the substrate, so their resonances merge into one wide stop band.

## 0.1 Design Goal
- This is a **millimeter wave** design. Millimeter waves run from 30 to 300 GHz.
- **Goal:** a wide stop band, simulated from 30 to 80 GHz.
- **Substrate:** Rogers RO4003 (lossy), 0.508 mm thick.
- **Cell size:** only 1.9 mm, because the wavelength is about 5 mm at these frequencies.

- **Front:** a **Jerusalem cross**. Two crossed bars are joined with Add, then an end cap is added to each arm.
- **Back:** a **fan-shaped loop**. It's a square loop with each side extended by an arm that reaches the cell edge.
- Because the fan's arms reach the cell edge, the back pattern connects to its neighbors in a sheet.

> [!tip] Drawing on the back face
> Flip the view to see the back, but remember that +X and -X appear swapped. Back-face copper runs from Z = 0 to Z = -ct.

> [!warning] Slide correction
> The arm length on the slide is wrong. Use **1.325 mm** for the fan's arms, not 0.5325 mm.

<text x="733.0" y="288" font-size="13" fill="#a5adce" text-anchor="middle">frequency (GHz): S21 in dB</text>
<text x="755.2" y="86" font-size="14" fill="#c6d0f5" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">47.5 to 69 GHz</text>
</svg>

- With the cross alone, the surface has a **narrow** stop band near 56.4 GHz.
- With the fan added, the stop band runs from about **47.5 to 69 GHz**. That's 21.5 GHz wide, about 37% of its center frequency.

> [!info] What's happening
> Each pattern adds its own resonance. When the resonances sit close together, their stop bands merge into a single wide one.

## 0.4 Building the Full Sheet
- It's built as in [[5. Bandstop FSS Design|Section 5]], with a Translate step of **L**.
- **Repetition factor 2** along X gives 3 cells, and one copy along Y makes 6.
- The results match the unit cell, as with the other FSS designs.

## 0.5 Parametric Analysis
- The cross width W was swept over 0.4, 0.5 and 0.6 mm on the unit cell.
- **Wider arms move the stop band higher, and narrower arms move it lower.** At W = 0.4 mm, the lower notch moved from about 47 GHz to about 44 GHz.

> [!info] Why wider arms raise the frequency
> The arm's length stays the same while it gets wider. A wider strip has **lower inductance**, and a lower inductance raises the resonant frequency. That's different from making a whole patch bigger.

## 0.6 Angle of Incidence
- theta was checked at 0° and 45°.
- At 45° the stop band moves lower, gets narrower, and the curve distorts slightly.
- It still works as a stop band, because S21 stays below S11. S11 itself barely changes.

## 0.7 FSS Designs Compared
| | Bandstop | Bandpass | Wideband |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Function** | Blocks the X band | Passes near 6.6 GHz | Blocks 47.5 to 69 GHz |
| **Front face** | Convoluted square loop | Loop and patch | Jerusalem cross |
| **Back face** | None | Same as front | Fan-shaped loop |
| **Substrate** | RT/duroid 5880 | FR-4 | RO4003 |
| **Cell size** | 6.8 mm, 0.23 λ | 32 mm, 0.7 λ | 1.9 mm, 0.37 λ |
| **Effect of angle** | Stable to 60° | Passband moves lower | Stop band narrows at 45° |

> [!tip] One workflow for all three
> Design the unit cell, simulate it, sweep the variables, check the angle, then build the sheet.
